oldowan-steinwerkzeuge#title: The First Stone Tools: the Oldowan
oldowan-steinwerkzeuge#summary: Early humans in East Africa strike sharp-edged flakes from stones, beginning the Stone Age.
oldowan-steinwerkzeuge#text: The oldest stones that can be identified with certainty as tools come from Gona in Ethiopia and are about 2.6 million years old; the technique is named after the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania. Using a hammerstone, early humans such as Homo habilis struck sharp flakes from cobbles and used them to strip meat from bones and to crack bones open for the nutritious marrow. Even older finds from Lomekwi in Kenya, roughly 3.3 million years old, suggest that pre-human species were already working with stones. Toolmaking is regarded as the beginning of the Stone Age and as a decisive step in human development.
homo-erectus-verlaesst-afrika#summary: The first human species to do so, Homo erectus spreads from Africa through the Near East as far as East Asia.
homo-erectus-verlaesst-afrika#text: About 1.8 million years ago, groups of Homo erectus reached the Caucasus, as the skull finds from Dmanisi in Georgia show. Over hundreds of thousands of years the species spread as far as Java and China, where it became known as Java Man and Peking Man, and later into Europe as well. An upright, enduring walker with a large brain, it made hand axes and learned to use fire. Homo erectus survived for roughly 1.8 million years, making it the longest-lived human species.
beherrschung-des-feuers#summary: Early humans learn to use fire deliberately and to keep it burning.
beherrschung-des-feuers#text: By about 400,000 years ago at the latest, humans of the species Homo erectus and their descendants were using fire regularly, as hearths in Africa, Israel and Europe show. Fire provided warmth and light, protected against predators and made food more digestible and more energy-rich through cooking. The shared fire became the center of the group and probably encouraged language and social life.
homo-sapiens-in-afrika#title: The Emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa
homo-sapiens-in-afrika#summary: Anatomically modern humans evolve in Africa.
homo-sapiens-in-afrika#text: The oldest known fossils of Homo sapiens come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 300,000 years old. Genetic studies confirm that all people alive today trace back to African ancestors. Modern humans were distinguished by a large brain, a flat face and a lightly built skeleton, and they produced increasingly refined tools.
blombos-hoehle-kunst-und-schmuck#title: Art and Ornament from Blombos Cave
blombos-hoehle-kunst-und-schmuck#summary: In South Africa, the oldest known geometric engravings and shell beads are created.
blombos-hoehle-kunst-und-schmuck#text: In Blombos Cave on the southern coast of South Africa, archaeologists found pieces of ochre engraved with diamond patterns, pierced snail shells worn as bead necklaces, and finely worked bone tools and spear points. The finds are around 75,000 years old, and a cross-hatched drawing made with ochre is about 73,000 years old. There was also a toolkit for mixing paint in abalone shells from a layer 100,000 years old. The cave shows that Homo sapiens was already thinking symbolically in Africa, long before cave art appeared in Europe.
auszug-aus-afrika#summary: Groups of Homo sapiens leave Africa and spread across Asia and Europe.
auszug-aus-afrika#text: About 70,000 to 60,000 years ago, small groups of modern humans migrated through the Near East into Asia and reached Europe around 45,000 years ago. There they encountered Neanderthals, with whom they occasionally interbred, as traces in the genomes of people today show. Within a few tens of thousands of years, Homo sapiens had settled almost the entire Old World.
besiedlung-australiens#summary: Humans reach the Australian continent by boat or raft.
besiedlung-australiens#text: At least 50,000 years ago, and according to some finds as early as 65,000 years ago, people crossed open stretches of sea from Southeast Asia to Australia. This is the earliest evidence of deliberate seafaring. Over tens of thousands of years the ancestors of the Aboriginal peoples developed a distinctive culture whose rock art is among the oldest artwork of humankind.
hoehlenmalerei-lascaux#summary: Ice Age hunters paint hundreds of animals on the walls of a cave in southern France.
hoehlenmalerei-lascaux#text: Discovered by teenagers in 1940, the cave of Lascaux in the Dordogne contains around 600 paintings and more than 1,000 engravings of horses, aurochs, deer and bison. The artists used pigments of ochre, charcoal and manganese ore and worked by the light of fat lamps. The images probably had religious or ritual meaning and show that people of the Old Stone Age were capable of symbolic thought and art.
erfindung-der-toepferei#summary: Hunter-gatherers in East Asia fire the first clay vessels, long before farming begins.
erfindung-der-toepferei#text: The world's oldest potsherds come from Xianrendong Cave in southern China and are about 18,000 to 20,000 years old; only slightly younger are finds from Japan, where the Jōmon culture later produced elaborately decorated vessels. Their makers were not yet farmers but hunters, fishers and gatherers who cooked food and stored supplies in clay pots. In the Near East and Europe, pottery only took hold with settled life around 7000 BC. Ceramics are especially important for archaeology because they last almost indefinitely and their shapes and patterns make individual cultures recognizable.
besiedlung-amerikas#summary: People from Siberia reach North America across the Bering land bridge.
besiedlung-amerikas#text: During the last Ice Age, sea levels were so low that a land bridge existed between Siberia and Alaska. Across it and along the Pacific coast, people migrated into the Americas and reached the southern tip of the continent within a few thousand years. The Americas were thus the last great landmass to be settled; the Indigenous peoples of the Americas descend from these migrants.
goebekli-tepe#title: Göbekli Tepe: the Oldest Monumental Structures
goebekli-tepe#summary: Hunter-gatherers in southeastern Anatolia erect stone circles with pillars weighing several tons.
goebekli-tepe#text: On the hill of Göbekli Tepe near the modern city of Şanlıurfa in Turkey, people built circular enclosures around 9500 BC from T-shaped stone pillars up to five meters high, carved with reliefs of animals. The builders still lived mainly by hunting and gathering. The site shows that communal sanctuaries may have arisen before farming and may have helped set the move toward settled life in motion.
neolithische-revolution#title: The Neolithic Revolution in the Fertile Crescent
neolithische-revolution#summary: People begin to grow grain and keep animals, and become settled.
neolithische-revolution#text: In the Fertile Crescent between the Levant, Anatolia and the Zagros Mountains, people began after the end of the Ice Age to cultivate emmer, einkorn, barley and lentils and to breed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. Instead of moving from place to place, they now lived permanently in villages of mud-brick houses. The shift to a farming way of life is regarded as one of the most profound changes in human history.
jericho-frueheste-stadtsiedlung#title: Jericho: One of the Oldest Settlements with a Wall
jericho-frueheste-stadtsiedlung#summary: A large permanent settlement grows up at a spring in the Jordan Valley and receives a stone wall and a tower around 8000 BC.
jericho-frueheste-stadtsiedlung#text: Jericho, today's Tell es-Sultan in the West Bank, was permanently settled around 9000 BC and soon grew to several hundred, perhaps more than a thousand inhabitants. Around 8000 BC the inhabitants surrounded their settlement with a stone wall and built a tower almost nine meters high with an internal staircase, the oldest known structure of its kind. Whether the wall served as protection against enemies or against floodwater and mud is disputed. Also famous are the plaster-covered skulls that represented ancestors and were kept in the houses. Jericho is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the world.
catalhoeyuek#summary: One of the largest settlements of the Neolithic, with several thousand inhabitants, arises in Anatolia.
catalhoeyuek#text: Çatalhöyük in central Anatolia was inhabited between about 7100 and 5700 BC and at times housed up to 8,000 people. The mud-brick houses stood packed together without streets and were entered through the roof by ladder. Wall paintings, bull skulls and female figurines offer insight into religious beliefs; the inhabitants practiced farming, kept livestock and traded in obsidian.
bewaesserungslandwirtschaft-mesopotamien: The First Irrigation Farming in Mesopotamia
Farmers channel river water onto their fields and make the dry land between the two rivers fertile.

In the regions along the middle Tigris there was too little rain for farming, but around 6000 BC villages of the Samarra culture such as Tell es-Sawwan and Choga Mami began to lead river water onto their fields through ditches. Artificial irrigation allowed two harvests a year, the cultivation of flax and grain, and larger settlements. Canals had to be dug, cleaned and shared collectively, which required agreement and leadership. On this foundation the world's first cities arose in southern Mesopotamia in the 4th millennium BC.
beginn-der-kupferzeit#title: The Beginning of Metalworking: the Copper Age
beginn-der-kupferzeit#summary: People learn to smelt copper ore and cast metal; the first copper axes, pins and ornaments appear.
beginn-der-kupferzeit#text: Native copper was already being cold-hammered in Anatolia around 8000 BC, but only around 5000 BC did smelting ore in furnaces succeed: the oldest evidence comes from Belovode in Serbia, shortly afterwards from Iran and Anatolia. The mines of Rudna Glava and the gold finds from the cemetery of Varna in Bulgaria show how quickly metal became a mark of wealth. Copper was soft and only of limited use for tools, but the knowledge of smelting and casting paved the way for the Bronze Age. In Europe this transitional period is called the Copper Age, and it was the age in which Ötzi lived.
domestizierung-des-pferdes#summary: On the steppes of Central Asia, people begin to keep, milk and ride horses.
domestizierung-des-pferdes#text: In settlements of the Botai culture in present-day Kazakhstan, researchers found large numbers of horse bones dating to around 3500 BC, traces of mare's milk in clay vessels, and wear on teeth suggesting the use of bits. Genetic studies show, however, that today's domestic horses descend from a different population from the steppes north of the Black Sea, which spread rapidly around 2200 BC. The horse fundamentally changed mobility, warfare and trade: riders and chariots shaped the Bronze Age, and pastoral peoples of the steppe were able to control vast territories.
erfindung-des-rades#summary: The first wheels and wagons appear almost simultaneously in Mesopotamia and Europe.
erfindung-des-rades#text: Around 3500 BC the oldest evidence for wheels appears: as a potter's wheel in Mesopotamia and as a wagon wheel in images and finds from the Near East to Central Europe. Solid wooden disc wheels on axles made ox-drawn carts possible and eased the transport of harvests, building material and goods. Together with the plow and copper working, the wheel began the transition to the advanced civilizations of the Bronze Age.
oetzi-stirbt-in-den-alpen#summary: A man of the Copper Age dies at the Tisenjoch pass and is preserved in the ice for more than 5,000 years.
oetzi-stirbt-in-den-alpen#text: In 1991, hikers at the Tisenjoch pass in the Ötztal Alps found the glacier mummy of a man who had died around 3300 BC. An arrow in his shoulder shows that he was killed. His clothing of fur and grass, his copper axe, bow and arrows, and the contents of his stomach provide unique information about life, diet and technology at the end of the Neolithic.
sumerische-keilschrift#summary: In the city of Uruk, the Sumerians develop the oldest known writing system.
sumerische-keilschrift#text: Around 3200 BC, scribes in Uruk began to record payments and stores with pictorial signs on clay tablets. The pictures became abstract signs pressed into damp clay in wedge shapes with a reed stylus. Cuneiform was used for more than 3,000 years for Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite and other languages, and it transmitted laws, contracts, myths and the Epic of Gilgamesh.
reichseinigung-aegyptens#summary: Upper and Lower Egypt are united under a single pharaoh.
reichseinigung-aegyptens#text: According to tradition, King Menes, who is probably identical with the ruler depicted on the Narmer Palette, united the Nile Valley from the First Cataract to the Delta. He is said to have founded the capital Memphis. This marked the beginning of pharaonic Egypt, which lasted with brief interruptions for almost three millennia and is divided into more than 30 dynasties.
megalithbauten-stonehenge#summary: Neolithic farmers in Western Europe build burial chambers, stone rows and stone circles from blocks weighing many tons.
megalithbauten-stonehenge#text: From about 4500 BC onward, people along the Atlantic coast from Portugal to Scandinavia built tombs and ritual sites from large stones, known as megaliths, among them the stone rows of Carnac in Brittany, the passage tomb of Newgrange in Ireland and the temples of Malta. Stonehenge in southern England began around 3000 BC as a circular ditch with wooden posts; around 2500 BC the sarsen stones, weighing up to 25 tons, were raised, while smaller bluestones came from Wales, 250 kilometers away. The monument is aligned with the sunrise at the summer solstice and probably served as a sanctuary and burial place. Structures like these required the cooperation of many communities over generations.
stadtstaaten-sumers-und-ur-standarte#tit: The City-States of Sumer and the Standard of Ur
stadtstaaten-sumers-und-ur-standarte#sum: In Sumer, city-states such as Ur, Uruk and Lagash compete for land and water; the royal tombs of Ur attest to their wealth.
stadtstaaten-sumers-und-ur-standarte#tex: In the 3rd millennium BC, Sumer was divided into a dozen city-states whose kings fought one another over canals, border land and supremacy; the Stele of the Vultures from Lagash depicts one of these wars. In the 1920s the British archaeologist Leonard Woolley uncovered the royal tombs of Ur, in which rulers had been buried with gold helmets, lyres, jewelry of lapis lazuli and dozens of sacrificed attendants. The so-called Standard of Ur, a box inlaid with shell and lapis lazuli, shows war with chariots on one side and a banquet with tribute on the other. The finds offer insight into kingship, craftsmanship and long-distance trade in the early city-states.
bau-der-cheops-pyramide#title: The Building of the Great Pyramid of Khufu
bau-der-cheops-pyramide#summary: The largest structure of antiquity is built at Giza as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu.
bau-der-cheops-pyramide#text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was originally about 146 meters high and consists of roughly 2.3 million blocks of stone. It was built in some 20 years by thousands of workers who were not slaves but paid and provisioned laborers. As the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, it testifies to the skill of Egyptian builders in planning, mathematics and organization.
bluete-der-indus-kultur#title: The Flowering of the Indus Civilization
bluete-der-indus-kultur#summary: Planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa arise along the Indus.
bluete-der-indus-kultur#text: The Indus Civilization extended across present-day Pakistan and northwestern India and covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia. Its cities had streets laid out at right angles, fired bricks, wells, baths and a sophisticated drainage system. The Indus script has still not been deciphered; around 1900 BC the cities declined, probably because of climate change and shifting rivers.
sargon-gruendet-akkadisches-reich#title: Sargon of Akkad Founds the First Empire
sargon-gruendet-akkadisches-reich#summar: Sargon subdues the Sumerian city-states and creates the first empire of Mesopotamia.
sargon-gruendet-akkadisches-reich#text: Sargon, who according to legend was abandoned as a foundling in a reed basket, conquered the city-states of Sumer around 2334 BC and extended his rule as far as Syria and Anatolia. He made Akkadian the language of administration and installed governors of his own. The Akkadian Empire lasted about 150 years and became the model for all later empires of Mesopotamia.
gilgamesch-epos#summary: The tales of King Gilgamesh of Uruk are written down and become the oldest great epic in world literature.
gilgamesch-epos#text: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh were written down around 2100 BC during the Third Dynasty of Ur; around 1200 BC the scribe Sin-leqi-unninni combined them in Babylonian into an epic on twelve tablets. It tells of the king's friendship with the wild Enkidu, of the fight against the monster Humbaba and of Gilgamesh's futile search for immortality after his friend's death. The eleventh tablet contains a flood story resembling the biblical account of Noah. The epic was copied in scribal schools from Anatolia to Palestine and was rediscovered in London in 1872 among tablets from the library of Ashurbanipal.
mittleres-reich-aegyptens#summary: After a period of collapse, Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt; a flowering of literature, administration and land reclamation follows.
mittleres-reich-aegyptens#text: After the collapse of the Old Kingdom and some 150 years of division, the Theban king Mentuhotep II reunified the country around 2055 BC. The kings of the 12th Dynasty, such as Senusret III and Amenemhat III, secured Nubia with fortresses, had large areas of the Fayum drained, and strengthened the officialdom against the nobility. The Middle Kingdom is regarded as the classical age of Egyptian literature, with works such as the Story of Sinuhe and the instructions for kings and officials. Around 1650 BC the Hyksos, who came from western Asia, took power in the Nile Delta and brought the horse and the chariot to Egypt.
minoische-kultur-auf-kreta#summary: With palaces such as Knossos, the first advanced civilization in Europe arises on Crete.
minoische-kultur-auf-kreta#text: From about 2000 BC the inhabitants of Crete built large palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, with hundreds of rooms, storage magazines, water pipes and brightly colored wall paintings of dolphins, bull-leapers and women in elaborate robes. The Minoans, named after the legendary King Minos, carried on sea trade as far as Egypt and Syria and wrote in Linear A, a script still undeciphered today. The absence of fortifications and of depictions of war is striking. The enormous volcanic eruption on the island of Thera around 1600 BC and the Mycenaean takeover around 1450 BC ended their heyday; Arthur Evans excavated Knossos from 1900 on.
codex-hammurapi#summary: King Hammurabi of Babylon has an extensive collection of laws carved in stone.
codex-hammurapi#text: On a stele of black diorite more than two meters high, Hammurabi had some 280 legal rulings recorded, covering family, property, trade, wages and punishments. The penalties depended on social rank and followed in part the principle of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. The stele was found at Susa in 1901 and stands today in the Louvre; it is one of the oldest and most complete collections of law in the world.
hethiter-reich#summary: From their capital Hattusa the Hittites rule Anatolia and northern Syria and become a great power alongside Egypt.
hethiter-reich#text: Around 1650 BC King Hattusili I made the mountain stronghold of Hattusa in central Anatolia his capital; his successor Mursili I even sacked Babylon in 1595 BC. The Hittites spoke the oldest Indo-European language preserved in writing, adopted cuneiform and left behind at Hattusa an archive of more than 30,000 clay tablets containing laws, treaties, rituals and myths. Their chariots and their early ironworking made them feared warriors; under Suppiluliuma I and Muwatalli II they struggled with Egypt over Syria. Around 1200 BC the empire collapsed in the turmoil of the Bronze Age collapse, and Hattusa was abandoned.
erdwerke-von-poverty-point#summary: Hunter-gatherers on the lower Mississippi build one of the largest earthwork complexes in North America.
erdwerke-von-poverty-point#text: In what is now Louisiana, people created six concentric, semicircular earthen ridges and several large mounds between about 1600 and 1100 BC. Remarkably, the builders were not farmers but lived from fishing, hunting and gathering wild plants. Stone, copper and other raw materials reached Poverty Point from hundreds of kilometers away, and the site was probably a meeting place for trade and ceremonies. Since 2014 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
mykenische-kultur#summary: On the Greek mainland warrior princes build citadels such as Mycenae and Pylos and administer them using the Linear B script.
mykenische-kultur#text: From about 1600 BC fortified palace citadels arose in Greece at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes, whose rulers were buried in shaft graves with gold masks and weapons. The Mycenaeans took over much from the Minoans but were more warlike: walls of blocks weighing many tons, the Lion Gate of Mycenae and beehive tombs testify to their power. Their script Linear B, deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, proved to be an early form of Greek and served to record stores, craftsmen and levies. Heinrich Schliemann excavated Mycenae in 1876 and believed he had found the world of Homer; around 1200 BC the palaces were destroyed, and Greece sank into a dark age.
shang-dynastie-orakelknochen#title: The Shang Dynasty and the Oracle Bones
shang-dynastie-orakelknochen#summary: In China the first archaeologically attested dynasty begins, with bronze casting and the oldest Chinese characters.
shang-dynastie-orakelknochen#text: The Shang dynasty ruled the valley of the Yellow River from about 1600 to 1046 BC. Its kings consulted the ancestors by heating ox shoulder blades and turtle shells and interpreting the cracks; the questions incised on them are the oldest evidence of Chinese writing. Elaborate bronze vessels, chariots and the royal tombs at Anyang reveal a highly developed and strictly ordered society.
lapita-besiedlung-pazifik#title: The Lapita Culture Settles the Pacific Islands
lapita-besiedlung-pazifik#summary: Seafarers with outrigger canoes set out from Southeast Asia and reach the remote islands of Melanesia and Polynesia.
lapita-besiedlung-pazifik#text: Around 1500 BC groups from the region of Taiwan and the Philippines pushed out through the Bismarck Archipelago into the open Pacific. They are recognizable by their stamped pottery, named after the site of Lapita in New Caledonia, and carried pigs, chickens and dogs as well as taro and yams in their canoes. Within a few centuries they reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, from where their descendants, the Polynesians, much later settled Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand. Navigating by stars, swells and the flight of birds across thousands of kilometers ranks among the greatest achievements in the history of seafaring.
echnatons-religionsreform#summary: Pharaoh Akhenaten raises the sun disk Aten to be the only god and founds a new capital.
echnatons-religionsreform#text: Amenhotep IV took the name Akhenaten, banned the worship of the old gods, above all Amun, and had a new residence, Akhetaten, built near present-day Amarna. The art of this period shows the king and his wife Nefertiti in an unusually natural and intimate manner. After his death Egypt returned to the old cults under Tutankhamun and erased Akhenaten's name from the monuments.
schlacht-bei-kadesch#title: The Battle of Kadesh and the First Peace Treaty
schlacht-bei-kadesch#summary: Egyptians and Hittites fight over Syria with thousands of chariots and later conclude the oldest surviving peace treaty.
schlacht-bei-kadesch#text: At Kadesh on the Orontes the armies of Ramesses II and of the Hittite king Muwatalli II clashed in one of the largest chariot battles in history. Ramesses only narrowly escaped defeat but had the battle portrayed in his temples as a brilliant victory. Some 15 years later Ramesses and Hattusili III concluded a treaty of peace and mutual assistance that survives on silver tablets and clay tablets and is regarded as the first peace treaty in world history.
ende-der-bronzezeit-seevoelker#title: The End of the Bronze Age and the Sea Peoples
ende-der-bronzezeit-seevoelker#summary: Within a few decades the Hittite Empire, the Mycenaean palaces and many trading cities collapse.
ende-der-bronzezeit-seevoelker#text: Around 1200 BC the Hittite Empire, the palaces of the Mycenaeans in Greece and cities such as Ugarit were destroyed or abandoned; Egypt fended off attacks by the so-called Sea Peoples only with difficulty. The causes are thought to be a combination of droughts, famines, earthquakes, uprisings and the breakdown of the trade networks for tin and copper. The crisis was followed by a dark age, out of which a new world emerged with iron tools and the alphabet of the Phoenicians.
beginn-der-eisenzeit#title: The First Ironworking and the Beginning of the Iron Age
beginn-der-eisenzeit#summary: After the collapse of the Bronze Age, iron, which is more readily available, becomes the standard material for weapons and tools.
beginn-der-eisenzeit#text: Individual iron objects made of meteoric iron are known as early as the 3rd millennium BC, and the Hittites produced small quantities of forged iron in the 14th century BC. Only when the trade routes for tin broke down around 1200 BC did smiths in Anatolia, Cyprus and the Levant turn on a larger scale to smelting iron ore in bloomery furnaces and improving the metal into steel by carburizing and hardening. Iron ore was available almost everywhere, so plowshares, axes and swords became cheaper. From the Near East the technique spread to Greece, Europe and India and, independently of this, to Africa south of the Sahara.
olmeken-in-mesoamerika#summary: The first advanced civilization of the Americas arises on the Gulf coast of Mexico.
olmeken-in-mesoamerika#text: From about 1200 BC the Olmecs built centers such as San Lorenzo and La Venta, with earthen pyramids, plazas and colossal heads of basalt weighing many tons. They grew maize, carried on long-distance trade in jade and obsidian, and played a ritual ball game. The calendar, the pantheon and the architectural forms of the Olmecs went on to influence the later cultures of the Maya and the Aztecs, which is why they are regarded as the mother culture of Mesoamerica.
phoenizier-und-alphabet#summary: The trading cities of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos develop an alphabet of 22 letters and carry it across the whole Mediterranean.
phoenizier-und-alphabet#text: Around 1050 BC the Phoenicians on the coast of present-day Lebanon simplified older consonant scripts of the Levant into an alphabet of only 22 signs that anyone could learn in a short time; the inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos is one of the earliest examples. As skilled seafarers and traders in purple dye, cedar wood, glass and metals, they founded settlements on Cyprus and Sicily, in Spain, and in 814 BC Carthage in North Africa. The Greeks adopted their letters and added vowels, the Etruscans and Romans passed them on; the Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic scripts also derive from the Phoenician alphabet.
koenigreich-kusch#title: The Kingdom of Kush in Nubia
koenigreich-kusch#summary: South of Egypt an independent African kingdom with its capital at Napata arises on the Nile.
koenigreich-kusch#text: Nubia, in what is now Sudan, was rich in gold and lay on the trade routes for ivory, ebony and incense. After the earlier kingdom of Kerma, which had been conquered by Egypt around 1500 BC, the Kingdom of Kush formed from about 1000 BC at Napata by the fourth cataract of the Nile. Its kings worshipped the god Amun at the sacred mountain Jebel Barkal and adopted hieroglyphs and pyramid tombs, yet remained culturally distinct. Around 730 BC the Kushite king Piye conquered Egypt and founded the 25th Dynasty of the Black Pharaohs; later Kush moved its capital to Meroe and lasted into the 4th century AD.
neuassyrisches-reich#summary: From Ashur and Nineveh the Assyrians conquer the entire Near East with the most powerful army of their day.
